Alpers|title=Ivory and Slaves: Changing Pattern of International Trade in East Central Africa|date=1975|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=978-0-520-02689-6|page=88|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uKYYwVTyOm0C&q=virji+vora&pg=PA88|access-date=4 February 2015|quote=In the early 1660s, Surat merchants had 50 ships trading overseas, and the wealthiest of these, Virji Vora had an estate valued at perhaps 8 million rupees...}} Gujaratis have earned a reputation as merchants, industrialists and business [[entrepreneur]]s{{cite book|last1=Mehta|first1=Makrand|title=Indian merchants and entrepreneurs in historical perspective : with special reference to shroffs of Gujarat, 17th to 19th centuries|date=1991|publisher=Academic Foundation|location=Delhi|isbn=978-8171880171|pages=21, 27|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9lz3gNDMbWEC&q=gujarati+business,+ancient&pg=PA21|access-date=29 October 2015|quote=The Gujarat region situated in the western part of India is known for its business activities since ancient times. So renowned had the Gujaratis become for their entrepreneurial spirit, commercial networks, and business acumen that a bill of credit issued by a Gujarati merchant would be honored as far as 5,000 miles away merely on the strength of the community's business reputation. Under Portuguese rule, the Indian Ocean trading system went into precipitous decline, and not until the nineteenth century did the Gujarati diaspora find a new lease of life. Gujarati traders migrated under the British dispensation in large numbers to Kenya, Tanganyika, South Africa, and Fiji, among other places, and Mohandas Gandhi, himself a Gujarati, has recorded that the early political proceedings of the Indian community in South Africa were conducted in the Gujarati language. In East Africa their presence was so prominent that banknotes in Kenya, before the country acquired independence, had inscriptions in Gujarati. Khojas, or Gujarati Ismailis, flourished and even occupied positions as teachers and educators in Muslim countries around the world.}} In recent decades, larger numbers of Gujaratis have migrated to [[English-speaking world|English-speaking countries]] such as the [[United States]] (especially [[New Jersey]]), [[United Kingdom]], [[Australia]], [[New Zealand]], and [[Canada]].{{cite book|title=Seeing Krishna in America The Hindu Bhakti Tradition of Vallabhacharya in India and Its Movement to the West.|date=2014|publisher=McFarland Publishing|isbn=9780786459735|pages=48, 49|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BWQMBAAAQBAJ&q=gujarati+migration,+america&pg=PA49|access-date=24 October 2015|quote=Among Gujaratis, emigration from India has a long history that has also affected Pushtimargiyas. Gujaratis may become the most transnational of groups because they assimilate selectively into the U.S. and maintain strong sending-country attachments}} ==History== {{Main|History of Gujarat}} [[File:Ludovico-di-Varthema-King-of-Khambat-16th-century-India.jpg|thumb|The king of Cambay (in present-day Gujarat) from "Figurae variae Asiae et Africae," a 16th-century Portuguese manuscript in the Casanatense Library in Rome (Codex Casanatense 1889)]] In anthropological surveys conducted in India about 60% of the people claim that their community is a migrant to their state or region. In Gujarat that number is around 70%. In the state, 124 Hindu communities out of 186 claim a migrant past. For example, the [[Audichya Brahmins]] claim migration from present day Uttar Pradesh. With Muslims in Gujarat, 67 out of 86 communities claim a migrant past.{{cite book|author1=Acyuta Yājñika|author2=Suchitra Sheth|title=The Shaping of Modern Gujarat: Plurality, Hindutva, and Beyond|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wmKIiAPgnF0C&pg=PR9|year=2005|publisher=Penguin Books India|isbn=978-0-14-400038-8|pages=2–3}} Early European travellers like [[Ludovico di Varthema]] (15th century) travelled to Gujarat and wrote on the people of Gujarat. He noted that [[Jainism in Gujarat|Jainism]] had a strong presence in Gujarat and opined that Gujaratis were deprived of their kingdom by Mughals because of their kind heartedness. His description of Gujaratis was:André Wink (1997) ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=75FlxDhZWpwC&q=heathens&pg=PA434 Al-Hind, the Making of the Indo-Islamic World: The Slavic Kings and the Islamic conquest]'', BRILL {{ISBN|90-04-10236-1}} pp.355–356 {{cquote|...a certain race which eats nothing that has blood, never kills any living things... and these people are neither moors nor heathens... if they were baptized, they would all be saved by the virtue of their works, for they never do to others what they would not do unto them.}} In 1790 and 1791, an epidemic devastated numerous parts of Gujarat during which 100,000 Gujaratis were killed in [[Surat]] alone.{{cite book|page=193|title=Eighteenth-Century Gujarat: The Dynamics of Its Political Economy, 1750-1800|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=En_heITTXCoC&pg=PA193|author=Ghulam A. Nadri|isbn=978-9004172029|year=2009|publisher=BRILL }} An outbreak of [[bubonic plague]] in 1812 has been claimed to have killed about half the Gujarati population.{{cite book|author1=Eskild Petersen|author2=Lin Hwei Chen|author3=Patricia Schlagenhauf-Lawlor|title=Infectious Diseases: A Geographic Guide|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VPEjDgAAQBAJ&pg=PA8|date=14 February 2017|publisher=Wiley|isbn=978-1-119-08573-7|page=8}}{{Cite journal |date=July 1906 |title=The Indian Medical Gazette July 1906 |journal= |issue=The Indian Medical Gazette |s2cid=33053536 }} ===Gujarati mercantile history=== Ports on the western coast of India have been engaged in trade for millennia. During the medieval and early modern period, ports in Gujarat such as [[Diu, India|Diu]], [[Surat]], [[Mandavi]], [[Cambay]], and [[Porbandar]] became important. Gujarati merchants operating from these ports operated not only in the Indian Ocean in the west but also in Southeast Asia. It is estimated that there were 1000 Gujarati merchants resident in [[Malacca]] in fifteenth century with a thousand others operating in the [[Bay of Bengal]] and [[Indonesian archipelago]]. Most of the Gujarati traders were Muslims but there were Hindu and Jains too despite religious prohibitions.{{Cite journal |last=McPherson |first=Kenneth |date=1988 |title=Maritime Passenger Traffic in the Indian Ocean Region Before the Nineteenth Century |url=http://www.jstor.org/stable/41562611 |journal=The Great Circle |volume=10 |issue=1 |pages=49–61 |jstor=41562611 |issn=0156-8698}} Gujarati merchants operating in Southeast Asia were primarily involved exporting India cotton to Southeast Asia in exchange for spices from the islands which were then exported to Persia. Surat was the principal port for this trade.Tracy, J. D. (1999). Asian Despotism? Mughal Government as Seen From the Dutch East India Company Factory in Surat. Journal of Early Modern History, 3(3), 256-280. {{doi|10.1163/157006599X00260}} Gujaratis played a big part in the Indian ocean trade. The Portuguese explorer [[Vasco de Gama]] noted presence of Muslim and Hindu navigators and merchants from Gujarat in [[Zanzibar]] and [[Pemba Island|Pemba]] and along the [[East Africa]] coast in towns such as [[Kilwa]], [[Bagamoyo]], [[Mombasa]] and [[Malindi]].{{Cite journal |last=Mehta |first=Makrand |date=2001 |title=Gujarati Business Communities in East African Diaspora: Major Historical Trends |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4410637 |journal=Economic and Political Weekly |volume=36 |issue=20 |pages=1738–1747 |jstor=4410637 |issn=0012-9976}} International trade by Gujarati merchants increased with the advent of the Gujarat Sultanate at the beginning of the 1400s. The trade involved gold, ivory and [[Slavery in India|slaves]] from Africa in exchange for cotton and glass beads from India.{{Cite journal |last=Alpers |first=Edward A. |date=1976 |title=Gujarat and the Trade of East Africa, c. 1500-1800 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/217389 |journal=The International Journal of African Historical Studies |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=22–44 |doi=10.2307/217389 |jstor=217389 |issn=0361-7882|url-access=subscription }} The important Gujarati traders active in the Indian Ocean trade at different periods of history included Jains; Hindu Bhatias and Lohanas; Muslim Khojas, Memons, and Bohras; and the Parsee communities. The Jains were active during the Solannki period trading with Arabian and Red sea ports. The Portuguese also preferred Jains to the Arab traders.{{Cite journal |last=Maloni |first=Ruby |date=2003 |title=Straddling the Arabian Sea: Gujarati Trade with West Asia 17th and 18th Centuries |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/44145498 |journal=Proceedings of the Indian History Congress |volume=64 |pages=622–636 |jstor=44145498 |issn=2249-1937}} ==Social stratification== Orthodox Gujarati society, which was [[mercantile]] by nature,{{cite web|title=Gujarat & India Same, Different But Same|url=http://www.outlookindia.com/magazine/story/gujarat-india-same-different-but-same/290783|website= outlookindia.com|date=5 February 2022 |quote=A historically mercantile culture, widespread influence of non violent Jainism, for the diluted casteism and an intrinsic irreverence makes society and polity in Gujarat different from other Indian states. Centre-right in their economic leaning, people here naturally gravitate towards leaner governments with high standards of governance... Absence of local rulers’ courts meant that trade-mercantile guilds ran affairs and administration. The kind of socio-cultural influence that pervaded the feudal kingdoms of Rajasthan etc was absent in Gujarat. The trade guilds were akin to the influential mercantile guilds of Belgium and the Netherlands, which contributed to making the Dutch world leaders in finance. In Gujarat, this cascaded into a strong entrepreneurial culture. As the English philosopher Bertrand Russell puts it, governments which consist of mercantilists tend to be more prudent in running the administration.}} was historically organised along [[ethno-religious]] lines and shaped into existence on the strength of its [[Mahajan]] ("[[guilds in India|guild]] assemblies"),{{cite book|last1=Jacobsen|first1=Knut A.|title=Routledge Handbook of Contemporary India|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781317403586|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=--9WCgAAQBAJ&q=mahajan,+gujarati&pg=PA275|language=en|date=11 August 2015}}{{cite book|last1=Pearson|first1=Michael Naylor|title=Merchants and Rulers in Gujarat: The Response to the Portuguese in the Sixteenth Century|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=9780520028098|url=https://archive.org/details/merchantsrulersi0000pear|url-access=registration|page=[https://archive.org/details/merchantsrulersi0000pear/page/124 124]|language=en|quote=Mahajan means different things in different parts of India; it can refer to an individual banker, a money-lender, a merchant, or an unspecified "great man." In Gujarat it usually meant a body representing a group of people engaged in the same commercial occupation, a governing council with an elected or occasionally hereditary headman...|date=1 January 1976}} and for its institution of Nagarsheth ("head of the guild assembly"); a 16th-century [[Mughal Empire|Mughal]] system akin to medieval European [[guilds]] which self-regulated the mercantile affairs of multi-ethnic, multi-religious communities in the Gujarati [[bourgeoisie]] long before municipal state politics was introduced.{{cite news|title=Going global|url=https://www.economist.com/news/christmas-specials/21683983-secrets-worlds-best-businesspeople-going-global|newspaper=The Economist|date=19 December 2015|quote=Whereas one religion, Protestantism, has often been associated with the rise of Anglo-Saxon capitalism, Gujarati capitalism was much more a fusion of influences. Ethnic and religious diversity became a source of strength, multiplying the trading networks that each community could exploit. Pragmatism and flexibility over identity, and a willingness to accommodate, perhaps inherited from the mahajans, are strong Gujarati traits, argues Edward Simpson of the School of Oriental and African Studies at the University of London. Gujaratis have been adept at remaining proudly Gujarati while becoming patriotically British, Ugandan or Fijian—an asset in a globalised economy.}}{{cite book|last1=Sundar|first1=Pushpa|title=Business and Community: The Story of Corporate Social Responsibility in India|publisher=SAGE Publications India|isbn=9788132111535|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=seiICwAAQBAJ&q=mahajan,+gujarati&pg=PA55|language=en|quote=The merchants were organized into mahajans or guilds with hereditary seths. A mahajan could include merchants of different religions and there was no strict segregation of religious, social, and occupational functions.|date=24 January 2013}} Historically, Gujaratis belonging to numerous faiths and [[castes]], thrived in an inclusive climate surcharged by a degree of [[cultural syncretism]], in which Hindus and [[Jains]] dominated occupations such as [[Banker|shroff]]s and brokers whereas, [[Gujarati Muslims|Muslims]], [[Hindu]]s and [[Parsi]]s largely dominated sea shipping trade. This led to religious [[interdependence]], tolerance, [[Cultural assimilation|assimilation]] and [[community cohesion]] ultimately becoming the hallmark of modern-day Gujarati society.{{cite book|last1=Rai|first1=Rajesh|last2=Reeves|first2=Peter|last3=Pro|first3=Visiting Professor Coordinator South Asia Studies Programme Peter Reeves|title=The South Asian Diaspora: Transnational Networks and Changing Identities|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781134105953|page=41|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bwJD2WBNtNMC&q=gujarat+muslims,+shipping&pg=PA41|language=en|quote=For Banias and Muslims there was a clear division of commercial activities based on religious persuasions and canonical injunctions. For example, Muslim merchants did not deal in printed textiles with motifs of living creatures on it, while these were procured by the Bania and Jain brokers. On the other hand Bania and Jain merchants would not deal in the trade of animals while Muslims did not have any problems with such trade. Similarly, Muslim merchants dominated the shipping trade and many were big ship-owners. The nakhudas and the lascars were also primarily from the Muslim community. On the other hand, some of the Banias and the Jains were prominent merchants and they organized an extensive trade from Gujarat to other parts of Asia. Thus, two forms of trade which formed the shipping and commerce were controlled by these two major communities of Gujarati merchants. For both these communities their relationship necessitated mutual understanding and interdependence in commercial matters so that they could play a complementary role in advancing their trading interests|date=25 July 2008}}{{cite book|last1=Malik|first1=Ashish|last2=Pereira|first2=Vijay|title=Indian Culture and Work Organisations in Transition|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781317232025|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hCUFDAAAQBAJ&q=gujarati,+society&pg=PA190|language=en|quote=He found that Gujaratis are highly family-oriented valuing family network and highly familial. They are also spiritualistic, religious and relationship oriented, attaching importance to co-operation. They are accepted to be materialistic. Panda, on the basis of empirical evidence, has named the society as 'collectivist familial (clannish) society'. Further, Gujarati society is found to have a high social capital. The dominant cultural characteristics identified from this study, which are essentially 'familial', 'co-operative' and 'non-hierarchical' (democratic) are consistent with Joshi's findings.|date=20 April 2016}}{{cite book|last1=Berger|first1=Peter|last2=Heidemann|first2=Frank|title=The Modern Anthropology of India: Ethnography, Themes and Theory|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1134061112|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sBgLb8XIGR8C&q=gujaratis,+uk,+anthropology+of+india&pg=PA84|language=en|quote=Gujaratis continuously redefine and contest caste and hiearchical values in a competitive pluralistic social environment. [[Patel|Patidars]] form the largest community in the diaspora including Kutch Leva Patels,{{cite web|title=Shree Kutch Leva Patel Community (UK)|url=http://www.sklpc.com/|website=sklpc.com/}} followed closely by [[Lohanas]] of [[Saurashtra people|Saurashtra]] origin.{{cite book|author1=Eliezer Ben Rafael, Yitzhak Sternberg|title=Transnationalism: Diasporas and the Advent of a New (Dis)order|isbn=978-90-04-17470-2|page=531|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QmpgywaZrrgC&q=gujarati+patidars,+lohanas,+UK&pg=PA531|access-date=4 February 2015|year=2009|publisher=BRILL }} Gujarati [[Rajputs]] from various regional backgrounds are affiliated with several independent British organisations dependent on caste such as Shree Maher Samaj UK,{{cite web|title=Shree Maher Samaj UK|url=http://www.maheronline.org/centres/shree-maher-samaj-uk|website=maheronline.org/|access-date=3 April 2015}} and the Gujarati Arya Kshatriya Mahasabha-UK.{{cite web|title=Gujarati Arya Kshatriya Mahasabha-UK|url=http://www.gakm.co.uk/?p=about|website=gakm.co.uk/?p=about|access-date=3 April 2015}} Endogamy remains important to Gujaratis in UK with the existence of matrimonial services specifically dedicated to their community.{{Cite journal |last1=Pemberton |first1=Trevor J. |last2=Li |first2=Fang-Yuan |last3=Hanson |first3=Erin K. |last4=Mehta |first4=Niyati U. |last5=Choi |first5=Sunju |last6=Ballantyne |first6=Jack |last7=Belmont |first7=John W. |last8=Rosenberg |first8=Noah A. |last9=Tyler-Smith |first9=Chris |last10=Patel |first10=Pragna I. |date=September 2012 |title=Impact of restricted marital practices on genetic variation in an endogamous Gujarati group |journal=American Journal of Physical Anthropology |volume=149 |issue=1 |pages=92–103 |doi=10.1002/ajpa.22101 |issn=0002-9483 |pmc=3436606 |pmid=22729696 |bibcode=2012AJPA..149...92P }} The Gujarati Muslim society in the UK have kept the custom of Jamat Bandi, literally meaning communal solidarity. This system is the traditional expression of communal solidarity. It is designed to regulate the affairs of the community and apply sanctions against infractions of the communal code. Total Gujarati Canadian population ! 209,410{{efn|name=population}} ! {{Percentage | 209410 | 209410 | 2 }} |} {{clear}} ===East Africa=== Former British colonies in East Africa had many residents of [[South Asian]] descent. The primary immigration was mainly from Gujarat and to a lesser extent from Punjab. They were brought there by the [[British Empire]] from [[British India|India]] to do [[clerk|clerical]] work in Imperial service, or unskilled and semi-skilled manual labour such as construction or farm work. In the 1890s, 32,000 labourers from British India were brought to the then British East African colonies under indentured labour contracts to work on the construction of the [[Uganda Railway]] that started in the Kenyan port city of [[Mombasa]] and ended in [[Kisumu]] on Kenyan side of [[Lake Victoria]]. Most of the surviving Indians returned home, but 6,724 individuals decided to remain in the [[African Great Lakes]] after the line's completion. Many Asians, particularly the Gujaratis, in these regions were in the trading businesses. They included Gujaratis of all religions as well many of the castes and Quoms. Since the representation of Indians in these occupations was high, stereotyping of Indians in Kenya, Uganda, and Tanganyika as shopkeepers was common. A number of people worked for the British run banks. They also worked in skilled labour occupations, as managers, teachers and administrators. Gujarati and other South Asians had significant influence on the economy, constituting 1% of the population while receiving a fifth of the national income. For example, in Uganda, the [[Nanji Kalidas Mehta|Mehta]] and [[Muljibhai Madhvani|Madhvani]] families controlled the bulk of the manufacturing businesses. Gated ethnic communities served elite healthcare and schooling services. Additionally, the tariff system in Uganda had historically been oriented toward the economic interests of South Asian traders.{{cite book|title= JSTOR}}<[https://www.jstor.org/discover/10.2307/160072?uid=3739936&uid=2129&uid=2&uid=70&uid=4&uid=3739256&sid=21101589093047 Expulsion of a minority: essays on Ugandan Asians.]> One of the oldest [[Jainism|Jain]] overseas diaspora was of Gujarat. Their number was estimated at 45,000 at the independence of the East African countries in the early 1960s.{{citation |last1=Gregory|first1=Robert G.|title=Quest for equality: Asian politics in East Africa, 1900-1967|date=1993|publisher=Orient Longman Limited|location=New Delhi|isbn=978-0-863-11-208-9|page=26|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Vl8tMabf5KUC&pg=PA1 }} Most members of this community belonged to Gujarati speaking Halari Visa Oshwal Jain community originally from the [[Jamnagar]] area of [[Saurashtra (region)|Saurashtra]].{{cite journal|last1=Mehta|first1=Makrand|title=Gujarati Business Communities in East African Diaspora: Major Historical Trends|journal=Economic and Political Weekly|date=2001|volume=36|issue=20|pages=1738–1747|jstor=4410637}} The countries of East Africa gained independence from Britain in the early 1960s. At that time most Gujarati and other Asians opted to remain as British Subjects. The African politicians at that time accused Asians of economic exploitation and introduced a policy of Africanization. The 1968 Committee on "Africanisation in Commerce and Industry" in Uganda made far-reaching Indophobic proposals. A system of work permits and trade licences was introduced in 1969 to restrict the role of Indians in economic and professional activities. Indians were segregated and discriminated against in all walks of life.{{cite journal |title=General Amin and the Indian Exodus from Uganda |first=Hasu H. |last=Patel |journal=Issue: A Journal of Opinion |volume=2 |issue=4 |year=1972 |pages=12–22 |doi=10.2307/1166488 |jstor=1166488 }} During the middle of the 1960s many Asians saw the writing on the wall and started moving either to UK or India. However, restrictive British immigration policies stopped a mass exodus of East African Asians until Idi Amin came to power in 1971. He exploited pre-existing Indophobia and spread propaganda against Indians involving stereotyping and scapegoating the Indian minority. Indians were stereotyped as "only traders" and "inbred" to their profession. Indians were labelled as "dukawallas" (an occupational term that degenerated into an anti-Indian slur during Amin's time), and stereotyped as "greedy, conniving," without any racial identity or loyalty but "always cheating, conspiring and plotting" to subvert Uganda. Amin used this propaganda to justify a campaign of "de-Indianization," eventually resulting in the expulsion and ethnic cleansing of Uganda's Indian minority. ====Kenya==== Gujarati and other Indians started moving to the Kenya colony at the end of the 19th century when the British colonial authorities started opening up the country with the laying down of the [[railroad]]s. A small colony of merchants, however, had existed on the port cities such Mombasa on the Kenyan coast for hundreds of years prior to that.{{cite news|author1=Parth Shastri|title=US researcher looks for Gujarati influence in Kenya and East Africa|url=http://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/ahmedabad/US-researcher-looks-for-Gujarati-influence-in-Kenya-and-East-Africa/articleshow/46816299.cms|website=the times of india|date=5 April 2015 |access-date=28 October 2015|quote=During British ascendancy, the early Gujarati-speaking traders were predominantly Muslims—Khoja, Bhora, and Ithna Asheri. They were quickly followed by Patel, Lohana, Bhatia and Oshawal. "Community was a major factor. It both energized Indian identity and simultaneously prevented Indians from coming together as a political whole except in times of dire crisis," Misha says.}} The immigrants who arrived with the British were the first ones to open up businesses in rural Kenya a century ago. These dukanwalas or shopkeepers were mainly Gujarati (Mostly Jains and Hindus and a minority of Muslims). Over the following decades the population, mainly Gujarati but also a sizeable number of Punjabi, increased in size. The population started declining after the independence of Kenya in the 1960s. At that time the majority of Gujaratis opted for British citizenship and eventually moved there, especially to cities like [[Leicester]] or [[London]] suburbs. And while some returned to sort out their affairs, very few went back for good.|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151110012925/http://blogs.new.spectator.co.uk/2012/12/ugandan-asians-are-part-of-britains-secret-weapon-for-success/|archive-date=10 November 2015}} In the late 19th century, mostly [[Sikhs]], were brought on three-year contracts, with the aid of Imperial British contractor [[Alibhai Mulla Jeevanjee]] to build the [[Uganda Railway]] from Mombasa to Kisumu by 1901, and to [[Kampala]] by 1931. After the 1972 expulsion, most Indians and Gujaratis migrated to the United Kingdom. Due to the efforts of the [[Aga Khan]], many Khoja Nizari Ismaili refugees from Uganda were offered asylum in Canada.{{cite web|title=Out of Africa: Thousands of Ismaili Muslims expelled from their African homelands in the 1970s have thrived in Canada|url=http://www.canada.com/calgaryherald/news/observer/story.html?id=4d43f2e2-2ccf-4234-96f4-35e853c20679|website=www.canada.com|publisher=Calgary Herald|access-date=28 October 2015|quote=Through the efforts of the Aga Khan, other countries agreed to take in the refugees, and they were scattered over the world. Indians in South Africa could traditionally be bifurcated as either indentured labourers (largely from Tamil Nadu, with smaller amounts from UP and Bihar) and merchants (exclusively from Gujarat). Yeh Hai India]]'' and ''[[Hum Dil De Chuke Sanam]]''. Dayro (gathering) involves singing and conversation reflecting on human nature. This literature is both in the form of poetry and prose.{{cite web|title=Shrimad Rajchandra – A spiritual gem|url=http://www.rajsaubhag.org/category/spiritual/foundations/shrimad-rajchandra/|website=www.rajsaubhag.org|access-date=27 October 2015|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140825134936/http://www.rajsaubhag.org/category/spiritual/foundations/shrimad-rajchandra/|archive-date=25 August 2014}} ===Cuisine=== {{Main|Gujarati cuisine}} [[File:Vedhmi.jpg|thumb|right|upright=0.9|''Vedhmi'' is a sweet lentil stuffed [[Roti|chapati]].]] Gujarati food has famously been described as "the haute cuisine of vegetarianism" and meals have a subtle balance of sweet, tart and mild hot sensations on the palate.{{cite book|last1=Jung|first1=Jeffrey Aldford & Naomi Duguid; photographs by Jeffrey Aldford & Naomi Duguid; additional photographs by Richard|title=Mangoes & curry leaves culinary travels through the great subcontinent|date=2005|publisher=Artisan|location=New York|isbn=9781579655655|page=14|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=K5viC1KaoBUC&q=meat+eating+in+gujarat&pg=PA14|access-date=24 October 2015}} Gujarati Jains, as well as many Hindus and [[Buddhists]] in Gujarat, are vegetarian. However, many Gujarati Hindu communities such as [[Ghanchi]], Koli Patel, and [[Kharwa caste|Kharwa]] consume fish as part of their diet.{{cite book |last1=Singh |first1=K.S. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4Cy_-FXW9BQC&dq=ghanchi++fish&pg=PR11 |title=People of India: Gujarat |publisher=Popular Prakashan |year=2003 |isbn=81-7991-104-7 |volume=22 |location=Mumbai, India |pages=397, 652, 694}} [[Christians]], and Muslims have traditionally eaten a variety of meats and seafood, although [[Muslim]]s don't eat pork and Hindus don't eat beef.{{cite web|author1=Zahir Janmohamed|title=Butter Chicken in Ahmedabad|url=http://india.blogs.nytimes.com/2013/08/20/butter-chicken-in-ahmedabad/|website=[[The New York Times]]|date=20 August 2013|access-date=24 October 2015|quote=But attitudes are changing, according to Mr. Dauwa. "More people, especially businessmen from China and Japan, are visiting Gujarat and many of them want non-vegetarian food," he said. "And also, Gujaratis are becoming wealthier, and when they live abroad they pick up nonvegetarian eating habits."|author1-link=The Racist Sandwich}} [[Gujarati cuisine]] follows the traditional Indian full meal structure of rice, cooked vegetables, [[dal|lentil dal]] or curry and ''[[roti]]''. The different types of flatbreads that a Gujarati cooks are [[rotli]] or [[chapati]], [[Bhakri|bhakhri]], puri, thepla, rotla, dhebara, maal purah, and puran-pohli. Popular snacks such as [[Khaman]], [[Dhokla]], Dhokli, dal-dhokli, [[Undhiyu]], [[Jalebi]], fafda, [[Chevda|chevdoh]], Muthia, Bhajia, Patra, bhusu, locho, sev {{Not a typo|usal}}, fafda gathiya, vanela gathiya and [[Sev mamra]], Sev Khaman, Dabeli are traditional Gujarati dishes savoured by many communities across the world.{{cite web|title=Western Indian Food: An explosion of Flavour|url=http://blog.mapsofindia.com/india/western-indian-food-an-explosion-of-flavour/|website=mapsofindia|access-date=27 October 2015}} [[Khichdi]] — a mix of rice and [[mung dal]], cooked with spice — is a popular and nutritious dish which has regional variations. Quite often the khichdi is accompanied by [[Kadhi]]. It is found satisfying by most Gujaratis, and cooked very regularly in most homes, typically on a busy day due to its ease of cooking. It can also become an elaborate meal such as a [[thali]] when served with several other side dishes such as a vegetable curry, yogurt, [[Indian cuisine|sabzi]] shaak, onions, mango pickle and [[papad]].{{cite book|last1=Hajratwala|first1=Bhanu|title=Gujarati kitchen : family recipes for the global palate|date=2011|publisher=Westland|location=Bangalore|isbn=9789380658490|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vTjBfwzuEYgC&q=gujarati+food+khichdi}} Spices have traditionally been made on grinding stones, however, since villages have seen rapid growth and industrialisation in recent decades, today people may use a blender or grinder. People from north Gujarat use dry red chili powder, whereas people from south Gujarat prefer using green chili and coriander in their cooking. There is no standard recipe for Gujarati dishes, however the use of tomatoes and [[lemons]] is a consistent theme throughout Gujarat.{{cite web|title=10 Best Gujarati Recipes|url=http://food.ndtv.com/lists/10-best-gujarati-recipes-695837|website=ndtv.com|access-date=27 October 2015}} Traditionally Gujaratis eat [[mukhwas]] at the end of a meal to enhance digestion, and desserts such as ''aam shrikhand'' made using [[mango]] salad and hung [[curd]] are very popular. In many parts of Gujarat, drinking [[chaas]] (chilled [[buttermilk]]) or soda after lunch or dinner is also quite common. Surti delicacies include [[ghari (sweet)|ghari]] which is a puri filled with [[khoa]] and nuts that is typically eaten during the festival [[Chandani Padva]]. [[Khambhat]] delicacies include famous [[sutarfeni]] — made from fine strands of sweet dough (rice or maida) garnished with pistachios, and ''halwasan'' which are hard squares made from broken wheat, khoa, nutmeg and [[pistachios]].{{cite book|author1=Darra Goldstein|title=The Oxford Companion to Sugar and Sweets Oxford Companions Series|date=2015|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0199313396|page=358|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jbi6BwAAQBAJ&q=gujarat,+cornstarch,+custard&pg=PA358}} A version of English [[custard]] is made in Gujarat that uses [[cornstarch]] instead of the traditional eggs. It is cooked with cardamom and [[saffron]], and served with fruit and sliced almonds.{{cite web|title=Sitafal basundi|url=http://www.khanakhazana.com/recipes/view.aspx?id=6361|website=khana khazana|access-date=25 October 2015}} Gujarati families celebrate [[Sharad Purnima]] by having dinner with doodh-pauva under moonlight.{{cite book|title=Passing on the Culture in the Diaspora: Inter-generational Communication of Cultural Identity Amongst Gujaratis in the USA.|date=2007|page=113|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=j5n5JDDhCZkC&q=gujarati+food,+doodh+pauva&pg=PA113|access-date=25 October 2015|isbn=9780549413127}} ===Folk dance and music=== The folk dances of Gujarat are [[Garba (dance)|Garba]], [[Dandiya]], [[Padhar dance|Padhar]], [[Tippani Dance|Tippani]], Dangi, etc. which are done during festivals.{{cite web | title=Notes make a culture|last=Patil|first=Vatsala | website=India Today| date=13 February 2015 | url=https://www.indiatoday.in/magazine/supplement/story/20150223-notes-make-a-culture-817538-2015-02-13 | access-date=3 October 2022}} [[File:Navratri Garba.jpg|thumb|upright=1.15|Women and men performing [[Garba (dance)|Garba]] as part of [[Navaratri]] celebrations in the city of Ahmedabad]] [[File:Mer Dandiya.jpg|thumb|upright=1.15|[[Mer people|Mer]] [[Dandiya]], a sword dance performed by the martial communities of [[Saurashtra (region)|Saurashtra]]]] === Gujarati folklore === Folklore is an important part of Gujarati culture. The folktales of Kankavati are religious in nature because they sprung from the ordinary day-to-day human cycle of life independent of, and sometimes deviating from the scriptures. They are part of the Hindu rituals and practices for marriage, [[Simantonnayana|baby shower]], [[Nāmakaraṇa|naming ceremony]], the harvest and death, and are not merely religious acts but they reflect the lived life of people in rural and urban societies. The anthologies of Dadaji Ni Vato and Raang Chhe Barot are pragmatic with practical and the esoteric wisdom. Saurashtra Ni Rasdhar is a collection of love legends and depicts every shade of love and love is the main emotion which makes human world beautiful because it calls forth patience, responsibility, sense of commitment and dedication. Also the study of Meghani's works is quintessential because he was a trailblazer in exploring the vast unexplored heritage of Gujarati folklore. His folktales mirror the milieu of Gujarat, dialects, duhas, decors, humane values, sense of sacrifice and spirit of adventure, enthusiasm and, of course, the flaws in people. extract: The Gujarati people, or Gujaratis, are an Indo-Aryan ethnolinguistic group native to the Indian state of Gujarat. They primarily speak Gujarati, an Indo-Aryan language. Gujaratis have diaspora across India as well as in a large number of countries around the world.
